title: Methods of studying human genetics: the genealogical, twin and population-statistical methods

goals.text: To teach the student the specific features of studying humans as a genetic object, the rules of drawing a pedigree and the criteria for determining the type of inheritance by the genealogical method, the assessment of the role of heredity and environment by the twin method, and the population-statistical method and the Hardy-Weinberg law.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the difficulties of studying human genetics and the system of methods;
the terms and symbols used in drawing a pedigree;
the criteria of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive and sex-linked inheritance;
monozygotic and dizygotic twins, concordance and Holzinger’s formula;
the concepts of population, deme and isolate and the Hardy-Weinberg law.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: draw and analyze a pedigree of one’s own family and from the conditions of a problem;
determine the type of inheritance and assess the risk for the next children;
calculate allele and genotype frequencies by the Hardy-Weinberg formula.

blocks.text: Human genetics obeys the laws of heredity common to all living organisms, but the classical hybridization method cannot be used to study humans. The reasons are:

items: experimental (purposeful) crossing is impossible in humans;
generations change slowly (25–30 years) and the number of children is small;
the karyotype is complex (46 chromosomes) and there are many linkage groups;
humans cannot be kept and observed under identical environmental conditions;
there are medical and ethical restrictions.

blocks.text: Therefore special methods are used in human genetics: the **genealogical, twin, population-statistical, cytogenetic, dermatoglyphic, biochemical, molecular genetic and immunogenetic** methods, somatic cell genetics and modeling. Human genetics also has advantages: the human phenotype and diseases are studied more deeply than in other organisms, populations are large, and written records exist for many generations.

The **genealogical method** (F. Galton, 1865) determines whether a trait is hereditary, its type of inheritance and the genotypes of family members by drawing and analyzing a pedigree. The method has two stages: collecting information and drawing the pedigree; genetic analysis of the pedigree.

blocks.title: Table 7.1. Basic terms of the genealogical method
head: Term
Meaning
rows: The person from whom the pedigree is started (usually the patient who consulted the doctor); shown with an arrow in the pedigree
Children of the same parents (brothers and sisters)
One row of the pedigree; numbered with Roman numerals, and the persons in each generation are numbered with Arabic numerals from left to right
A dot inside a circle or square, or a half-shaded symbol

blocks.label: Figure 7.1
blocks.caption: Main symbols used in drawing pedigrees: male (square), female (circle), affected (shaded), marriage, consanguineous marriage, sibs, twins, carriers, stillborn child and others (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

parts.text: Rule of drawing a pedigree: each generation is written in one horizontal row; the parents are joined by a marriage line, and the children are placed on a “sibship” line hanging from it in order of birth from left to right; a key (legend) to the symbols is given under the pedigree.

sections.title: 3. Criteria of the types of inheritance

blocks.title: Table 7.2. Criteria for determining the type of inheritance from a pedigree
head: Type
Main features
Examples
rows: The trait occurs in every generation (“vertical” transmission); at least one parent of an affected child is affected; males and females are affected equally; 50 % of children of an affected heterozygote and a healthy partner are affected
Polydactyly, achondroplasia, Marfan syndrome, Huntington disease, brachydactyly

The trait skips generations (“horizontal” transmission — among sibs); affected children are often born to healthy parents; the risk in a marriage of two carriers is 25 %; frequent in consanguineous marriages
Phenylketonuria, albinism, cystic fibrosis, Wilson disease, galactosemia
Mainly males are affected; the disease passes through the maternal line (uncles, nephews); not passed from father to son
Women are affected 2 times more often; all daughters of an affected father are affected, his sons are healthy
Only in males, from father to all sons

blocks.label: Figure 7.2
blocks.caption: Inheritance of a recessive trait (phenylketonuria): affected children are born to phenotypically healthy heterozygous (Aa) parents; the affected persons in generation IV come from a consanguineous marriage (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: The classic example of a hemophilia pedigree is the family of **Queen Victoria** of Great Britain (Figure 7.3). Victoria was a carrier of the hemophilia gene; her son Leopold was affected and her daughters Alice and Beatrice were carriers, and the gene spread to the royal families of Germany, Russia and Spain (the Russian heir to the throne Alexei also had hemophilia).

blocks.label: Figure 7.3
blocks.caption: Transmission of hemophilia — the descendants of Queen Victoria of Great Britain (shaded square — affected male, circle with a dot — carrier female) (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: The **twin method** (F. Galton, 1876) compares traits in monozygotic and dizygotic twins to determine the relative role of heredity and environment in their formation. Twins are born in about 1 % of human births.

blocks.title: Table 7.3. Types of twins
head: Feature
Monozygotic (identical, MZ)
Dizygotic (fraternal, DZ)
rows: One zygote splits into two at the early stages of cleavage
Two eggs are fertilized by two sperm
On average 50 % genes in common (like ordinary sibs)

blocks.text: The presence of a trait in both twins is called **concordance**, and its presence in only one is called **discordance**. The percentage of concordance is compared in MZ and DZ pairs: if concordance in MZ is much higher than in DZ, heredity plays an important role in the development of the trait. The **coefficient of heritability** is calculated by Holzinger’s formula:
Here C is the percentage of concordance, H the share of heredity and E the share of environment. If H > 0.7, the trait is determined mainly by heredity; if H < 0.4, mainly by the environment.

parts.text: In measles concordance is almost equally high in MZ and DZ — susceptibility to this disease depends mainly on the environment (contact with the virus). In schizophrenia and type 2 diabetes MZ concordance is much higher — these are **diseases with a hereditary predisposition (multifactorial)**.

blocks.text: A **population** is a group of individuals of one species living for a long time in a certain area and freely marrying each other. In humans small groups are distinguished within large populations: a **deme** (1500–4000 people, marriages within the group 80–90 %) and an **isolate** (up to 1500 people, marriages within the group more than 90 %). In isolates consanguineous marriages are common, so the frequency of recessive diseases rises (geographic, religious, ethnic isolates).

In a population of self-fertilizing organisms the proportion of heterozygotes halves in each generation and the population splits into homozygous lines. In cross-fertilizing (panmictic) populations the ratio of genotypes obeys the **Hardy-Weinberg law**:

Here p is the frequency of the dominant allele (A), q the frequency of the recessive allele (a), and p^2^, 2pq and q^2^ the frequencies of the genotypes AA, Aa and aa. The law holds for an **ideal population**: the population is large, mating is random (panmixia), and there are no mutations, natural selection or migration.

parts.text: Calculation always starts from the **recessive homozygotes**, because only their phenotype matches their genotype: for example, if phenylketonuria occurs at 1 : 10000, then q^2^ = 0.0001, q = 0.01 and p = 0.99; heterozygous carriers 2pq ≈ 0.02, i.e., one in every 50 people.

blocks.text: **Stages of the population-statistical method:** choosing the population, collecting data (frequency of the disease or trait), statistical analysis. The method is used to determine allele and genotype frequencies, the spread of hereditary diseases and carriers and their geographic and ethnic differences, the frequency of mutations, and to plan medical genetic services.

skills.title: Skill: drawing and analyzing a pedigree

items: Starting from the proband, collect information about the sibs, parents, grandparents and relatives on the father’s and mother’s sides (at least 3 generations).
Number the generations with Roman numerals and the persons in each generation with Arabic numerals.
Draw the pedigree with the standard symbols and mark the proband with an arrow.
Analyze whether the trait is present in every generation, whether it occurs in children of healthy parents and how it is distributed by sex.
Determine the type of inheritance and write the probable genotypes of the persons.
Calculate the risk of the disease for the next child.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: The proband is a boy with hemophilia; his parents are healthy. The proband’s maternal grandfather has hemophilia and his grandmother is healthy. Hemophilia has not been observed on the father’s side.
cases.ask: Draw the pedigree and determine the type of inheritance and the genotypes of the family members.
cases.answer: The disease occurs only in males and passes through the maternal line (grandfather → mother → grandson), with no father-to-son transmission — X-linked recessive type. Grandfather — X^h^Y, grandmother — X^H^X^H^; their daughter (the proband’s mother) is an obligate carrier — X^H^X^h^; the proband’s father — X^H^Y; the proband — X^h^Y. In this family the risk for later sons to have hemophilia is 50 %, and for daughters to be carriers 50 %.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: In a city 51 % of the population is brown-eyed and 49 % blue-eyed. Brown eyes (A) are completely dominant over blue eyes (a).
cases.ask: What are the frequencies of homozygous and heterozygous genotypes in the population?

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: Two populations of the same origin but living under different conditions differ sharply in the frequency of a certain recessive disease: 1 : 5000 in one and 1 : 50000 in the other.
cases.answer: The population with the higher frequency is probably an isolate or a deme: consanguineous marriages (inbreeding), gene drift and the “founder effect” (an allele that by chance was common in the small group from which the population descended) act in it. In such a population recessive alleles often become homozygous. In a large panmictic population there are few consanguineous marriages and the allele is expressed less often.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Dominant type — **“vertical”** (every generation), recessive type — **“horizontal”** (among sibs, skipping generations).

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Hardy-Weinberg is a squared binomial: **(p + q)^2^ = p^2^ + 2pq + q^2^** — AA, Aa, aa.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: Pedigree analysis is the basis of genetic counseling: it reveals the type of inheritance and the risk for the next child, while the twin method assesses the share of heredity in multifactorial diseases.
